targets: Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints
title: Mallet finger and boutonnière deformity
text:
The extensor mechanism of each finger divides over the proximal phalanx into a central slip, inserting on the base of the middle phalanx, and two lateral bands that reunite as the terminal tendon on the distal phalanx.
Mallet finger: forced flexion of the extended fingertip (a ball striking it) ruptures or avulses the terminal tendon, and the DIP joint droops and cannot be actively straightened. It is treated with a splint holding the DIP in extension continuously for 6 to 8 weeks (any flexion restarts the clock); a large bony fragment with joint subluxation needs fixation. Untreated, the imbalance produces a swan-neck deformity.
Boutonnière deformity: rupture of the central slip over the PIP joint (a laceration, or forced flexion of an extended PIP) lets the lateral bands slip below the joint axis, so the PIP flexes and the DIP hyperextends. It develops over 1 to 3 weeks, so a dorsal PIP injury needs checking for central slip function (Elson test) and a splint holding the PIP in extension with the DIP free. Rheumatoid arthritis causes both deformities by synovitis.

title: Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb (skier's and gamekeeper's thumb)
text:
Forced abduction of the thumb, as when a skier falls with the pole in the hand, tears the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint (chronic attenuation was described in gamekeepers). Pinch and grip are weak and painful, and the joint opens on radial stress testing: laxity of more than about 30 to 35 degrees, or 15 degrees more than the other side, with no firm end point indicates a complete tear (radiographs first to exclude an avulsion fracture).
In a Stener lesion the torn distal end of the ligament flips out and comes to lie superficial to the aponeurosis of adductor pollicis, which then blocks it from healing back to the bone. A Stener lesion (often a palpable lump over the ulnar side of the joint, confirmed by ultrasound) or a complete tear requires surgical repair; partial tears heal in a thumb spica splint. Untreated instability leads to weak pinch and arthritis.

title: Bennett and Rolando fractures
text:
A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal from an axial blow to the flexed thumb (a punch). A small volar-ulnar fragment remains attached to the trapezium by the strong anterior oblique (beak) ligament, while abductor pollicis longus pulls the shaft proximally and radially and adductor pollicis pulls it into adduction, so the carpometacarpal joint subluxes. The deforming forces make closed treatment unreliable: the fracture is reduced and fixed (percutaneous wires or screws) to restore the joint surface and prevent early arthritis of this key joint for opposition.
A Rolando fracture is a comminuted (Y- or T-shaped) intra-articular fracture of the same base, with a worse prognosis. Extra-articular fractures of the base tolerate much more angulation because of the mobility of the carpometacarpal joint.

title: Boxer's fracture and fight bite
text:
Punching a hard object fractures the neck of the fifth (and sometimes fourth) metacarpal, with the head tilting into the palm and a lost knuckle. Because the fourth and fifth carpometacarpal joints are mobile, considerable volar angulation (often quoted up to about 40 to 70 degrees for the little finger) is compatible with good function, but ROTATIONAL deformity is not: when the patient makes a fist, the fingers should point toward the scaphoid without overlapping (scissoring). Rotation or excessive angulation needs reduction and fixation; most are treated with buddy strapping and early movement.
A small wound over a metacarpophalangeal joint after a punch is a human bite ('fight bite') until proven otherwise: teeth penetrate the extensor tendon and capsule of the flexed joint, and the wound seals as the fingers extend. Mixed oral flora, including Eikenella corrodens, cause septic arthritis and tendon sheath infection, so these wounds need radiographs (tooth fragments, fractures), surgical exploration and washout, and antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav.

title: Scapholunate dissociation
text:
The scapholunate interosseous ligament is the key stabiliser of the proximal carpal row. It tears with a fall on the outstretched hand with the wrist extended and ulnarly deviated, often with a distal radius fracture, and is frequently missed as a 'sprain'.
Signs: dorsal wrist pain and swelling just distal to Lister tubercle, and a painful clunk on the Watson scaphoid shift test (pressure on the scaphoid tubercle while moving the wrist from ulnar to radial deviation). A posteroanterior radiograph (ideally a clenched-fist view) shows a scapholunate gap over about 3 mm (the 'Terry Thomas' sign) and a flexed, foreshortened scaphoid whose tubercle appears end-on as a ring (the signet ring sign); the lateral view shows the lunate tilted dorsally (dorsal intercalated segment instability). Acute tears are repaired; untreated, abnormal loading leads to the predictable pattern of scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC wrist) arthritis, starting between the radial styloid and scaphoid.

targets: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
title: Triangular fibrocartilage complex and ulnar-sided wrist pain
text:
The triangular fibrocartilage complex, centred on the articular disc between the distal ulna and the triquetrum and lunate, cushions the ulnar carpus and is the main stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint. It is torn by falls on the outstretched pronated hand and by rotational sports injuries, and degenerates with age.
Patients have ulnar-sided wrist pain worse on gripping, rotation and ulnar deviation, clicking, and tenderness in the soft spot between the ulnar styloid and flexor carpi ulnaris (ulnar fovea sign). Instability of the distal radioulnar joint shows as a prominent ulnar head that can be pushed down and springs back (piano key sign). In ulnar impaction syndrome a long ulna relative to the radius (positive ulnar variance, congenital or after a malunited distal radius fracture) grinds the disc and lunate. MR arthrography or wrist arthroscopy confirms tears; treatment is splinting, arthroscopic debridement or repair, or ulnar shortening osteotomy.

title: Essex-Lopresti injury
text:
The forearm is a ring: the radius and ulna are linked at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints and along their length by the interosseous membrane, whose central band transfers load from the radius (which receives most of the force at the wrist) to the ulna (which carries it at the elbow). A fall from height onto the outstretched hand can fracture the radial head and tear the interosseous membrane and the distal radioulnar joint ligaments together.
The distal injury is often missed because attention focuses on the radial head. If the comminuted radial head is simply excised, the radius migrates proximally, producing wrist pain, ulnar impaction and loss of rotation that is very difficult to salvage. Every radial head fracture therefore requires examination of the wrist and forearm, with bilateral wrist radiographs if there is tenderness, and the radial head is fixed or replaced with a prosthesis rather than excised when the ring is disrupted.

title: Lisfranc injury of the midfoot
text:
The base of the second metatarsal is recessed between the medial and lateral cuneiforms like a keystone, and the strong Lisfranc ligament runs obliquely from the medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal; there is no ligament between the bases of the first and second metatarsals. Injuries range from sprains of the ligament to fracture-dislocations from high energy trauma, a twisting fall on a plantarflexed foot or a crush.
Up to a fifth are missed initially. Clues: midfoot pain and inability to weight bear, plantar ecchymosis over the midfoot, and pain on passive pronation-abduction. On radiographs the medial border of the second metatarsal should line up with the medial border of the intermediate cuneiform (and the fourth metatarsal with the cuboid on the oblique view); a small avulsed fragment between the first and second metatarsal bases (fleck sign) or diastasis is diagnostic. Weight-bearing films or CT reveal subtle instability. Unstable injuries need anatomical reduction and fixation; delayed treatment leads to painful midfoot arthritis and flatfoot. The dorsalis pedis artery dives between the first and second metatarsals here and can be injured.

title: High ankle sprain and deltoid ligament rupture
text:
External rotation of the foot on a fixed leg (football, skiing) injures the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, especially the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, above the joint line: a 'high' ankle sprain. Pain and tenderness lie above the lateral ankle and are reproduced by squeezing the tibia and fibula together at mid-calf (squeeze test) or by externally rotating the foot with the knee flexed. Recovery takes much longer than for an ordinary inversion sprain.
The deltoid (medial collateral) ligament is the main restraint to lateral shift of the talus. With a lateral malleolar (Weber B) fracture, medial tenderness, bruising or a widened medial clear space between the talus and medial malleolus (over about 4 to 5 mm on a mortise or stress view) means the deltoid is ruptured and the ankle is effectively bimalleolar and unstable, needing fixation. A syndesmotic injury with widening of the tibiofibular clear space is fixed with screws or a suture button to restore the mortise.

title: Posterior ankle impingement and dancer's tendinitis
text:
Forced plantarflexion, as in ballet dancers on pointe, footballers kicking and downhill runners, compresses the soft tissue and bone between the back of the tibia and the calcaneus. An os trigonum (an unfused ossicle behind the lateral tubercle of the talus, present in about 7 to 14% of people) or an enlarged lateral tubercle (Stieda process) is the usual culprit, causing posterior ankle pain on plantarflexion that is reproduced by forced passive plantarflexion.
The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs in a fibro-osseous tunnel between the medial and lateral talar tubercles, so it is often inflamed alongside: pain behind the medial malleolus on resisted great toe flexion, and triggering or locking of the hallux when a nodule catches in the tunnel ('dancer's tendinitis'). Treatment is activity modification, image-guided injection, and arthroscopic or open excision of the ossicle with release of the tendon sheath.

title: Hallux valgus, hallux rigidus and sesamoid injury
text:
Hallux valgus: the first metatarsal drifts medially (metatarsus primus varus) while the great toe deviates laterally, pulled by adductor hallucis and the long flexors and extensors, which bowstring lateral to the joint axis. The sesamoids stay under the second metatarsal, so relative to the first metatarsal head they lie laterally; the exposed medial head forms a bunion with an overlying bursa. Risk factors are genetics, female sex, narrow shoes and hypermobility; symptomatic cases are corrected by metatarsal osteotomy.
Hallux rigidus is osteoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, with a dorsal osteophyte blocking dorsiflexion and pain on push-off (treated by cheilectomy or fusion). Gout typically attacks this joint first (podagra).
The two sesamoids within the flexor hallucis brevis tendons bear body weight during toe-off. They can fracture, develop stress injuries or avascular necrosis, and become inflamed (sesamoiditis); a bipartite medial sesamoid is a normal variant that mimics fracture. Forced hyperextension of the joint tears the plantar plate ('turf toe').

title: Anterior knee pain below the patella
text:
Patellar tendinopathy ('jumper's knee') causes pain and tenderness at the tendon origin on the inferior pole of the patella in volleyball and basketball players, worse with jumping, squatting and prolonged sitting; eccentric loading programmes are the mainstay of treatment. In adolescents the equivalent traction apophysitis at the inferior pole is Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome, while Osgood-Schlatter disease affects the tibial tuberosity.
The infrapatellar fat pad (Hoffa pad) is richly innervated; impingement between the femur and tibia in hyperextension causes pain on either side of the patellar tendon. Superficial infrapatellar bursitis ('clergyman's knee', from kneeling upright) causes a fluctuant swelling in front of the tendon, while the deep infrapatellar bursa lies between the tendon and the tibia and can be inflamed by overuse or Osgood-Schlatter disease. None of these restrict knee movement much, which helps distinguish them from a joint effusion. Patellar tendon rupture, usually in younger men at the inferior pole, produces a high-riding patella (patella alta) and loss of active knee extension.

title: Haglund deformity and insertional Achilles pain
text:
Two bursae lie at the back of the heel: the retrocalcaneal (subtendinous) bursa between the calcaneal tendon and the posterosuperior corner of the calcaneus, and the subcutaneous bursa between the tendon and the skin. A prominent posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity (Haglund deformity) compresses the retrocalcaneal bursa and tendon with each dorsiflexion, especially in rigid-backed shoes, while shoe friction inflames the superficial bursa ('pump bump').
Insertional Achilles tendinopathy causes pain at the tendon insertion, often with intratendinous calcification or a spur, and differs from mid-portion tendinopathy 2 to 6 cm above the insertion (the hypovascular zone where ruptures also occur). Bilateral heel enthesitis in a young adult suggests spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive or psoriatic arthritis); fluoroquinolone antibiotics and steroids predispose to tendinopathy and rupture. Treatment includes heel raises, shoe modification and eccentric exercises; resistant cases have resection of the prominence and debridement.

title: Internal snapping hip and iliopsoas bursitis
text:
The iliopsoas tendon passes over the iliopectineal eminence and the front of the femoral head and hip capsule on its way to the lesser trochanter, with the iliopectineal (iliopsoas) bursa, the largest bursa around the hip, between tendon and capsule. The bursa communicates with the hip joint in about 15% of adults, so a hip effusion from arthritis can present as a groin mass.
Internal ('coxa saltans interna') snapping is an audible clunk in the groin when the hip moves from flexion, abduction and external rotation into extension, as the tendon flicks over the bony prominences; it is common in dancers and usually painless. External snapping is the iliotibial band catching on the greater trochanter, and intra-articular snapping with pain and locking suggests a labral tear or loose body.
Iliopsoas bursitis causes deep anterior groin pain worse on resisted hip flexion; an enlarged bursa can compress the femoral vein or nerve. Dynamic ultrasound shows the snapping and guides injection; tendon lengthening is a last resort.

targets: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus
Synovial sheaths of digits of hand
title: Flexor sheath infection and the horseshoe abscess
text:
The synovial sheaths of the index, middle and ring fingers end at the level of the distal palmar crease, but the sheath of the little finger is continuous with the common flexor sheath (ulnar bursa) in the palm and carpal tunnel, and the sheath of flexor pollicis longus is continuous with the radial bursa. The two bursae may communicate in the carpal tunnel and in Parona's space in the distal forearm.
A puncture wound over a finger crease can inoculate the sheath. Kanavel's four signs of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis are: the finger held in slight flexion, uniform fusiform swelling, tenderness along the whole sheath, and severe pain on passive extension (the most sensitive). Infection of the little finger or thumb sheath can spread to the palm and across the wrist to the other, forming a 'horseshoe' abscess. It is a surgical emergency: without urgent IV antibiotics and sheath irrigation, pus under pressure destroys the gliding surfaces and the tendon's blood supply, leaving a stiff finger or tendon necrosis.

title: SLAP tears of the superior labrum
text:
The long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and the superior glenoid labrum. Repetitive overhead throwing (the 'peel-back' mechanism in late cocking), a fall on the outstretched arm or sudden traction tears the superior labrum from anterior to posterior (SLAP lesion), sometimes extending into the biceps anchor.
Patients describe deep, poorly localised shoulder pain with overhead activity, clicking or catching and a 'dead arm' feeling during throwing; the O'Brien active compression test is often positive, but clinical tests are unreliable. MR arthrography shows contrast tracking into the labral base. Normal anatomical variants such as a sublabral foramen or the Buford complex (absent anterosuperior labrum with a cord-like middle glenohumeral ligament) must not be mistaken for tears. A paralabral cyst extending from a posterior-superior tear can compress the suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch. Treatment ranges from rehabilitation to arthroscopic repair or biceps tenodesis, the latter favoured in older patients.

title: Posterior sternoclavicular dislocation
text:
The sternoclavicular joint is the only bony articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton; its articular disc and strong capsular and costoclavicular ligaments make dislocation rare. Anterior dislocation is commoner and mostly a cosmetic problem. Posterior (retrosternal) dislocation, from a blow to the front of the medial clavicle or a lateral compression force on the shoulder, drives the clavicle head backward toward the trachea, oesophagus, brachiocephalic vessels, subclavian artery and brachial plexus, causing dyspnoea, stridor, dysphagia, venous congestion of the arm or absent pulses.
Plain films are hard to interpret (the serendipity view helps), so CT with contrast is the investigation of choice. Posterior dislocation is reduced urgently under anaesthesia with a cardiothoracic surgeon available. In patients under about 25 years the medial clavicular physis, the last growth plate in the body to fuse, has not closed, and an apparent dislocation is often a physeal fracture, which remodels well.
